card.hook: Plot twist: the most dependable photo in Teahupo'o isn't of the famous wave at all. From the shore, the surf can look pretty small, so save your wow shot for the village sign.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Teahupo'o Wave Sign, at the village entrance near Teahupo'o Beach. The phone icon on the map is about 5.4 km east of the subject, so face west, with the coastline and green hills behind the sign.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the sign with the coast behind it. Want more hillside in the frame? Switch to zoom 0.5x. At the boat landing, try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pull in the boats and the surf beyond the lagoon.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the sign on one side, tap the sign, then slide darker if the sky is bright so the hills keep their green.
card.best_time: Surf season runs roughly May to October, and the wave is best seen at high tide with offshore winds. For the sign photo, morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light.
card.selfie_here: Do your selfie at the Teahupo'o Wave Sign on the road in the village, where you can park. A reviewer called it a good photo stop. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and tuck the sign over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the village beach to take your photo while you stand with the surf break and reef in view behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep to the shore and never walk on the reef.
card.challenge: Get the sign, the hills and one boat heading out through the channel in the same trip. Bonus points if you look like you surf.
card.good_to_know: Teahupo'o is a small village of roughly 1,500 people, served by a single one-lane road. The wave is so hollow because it breaks over a coral reef only about 51 cm (20 inches) below the surface in places. The village hosted the surfing at the 2024 Summer Olympics, a long way from Paris. Boat trips are paid and can be stopped on big-swell days, so ask locally.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Teahupo'o Wave Sign, at the village entrance near Teahupo'o Beach. The phone icon on the map is about 5.4 km east of the subject, so face west, with the coastline and green hills behind the sign.

selfie_spots.name: Teahupoo Wave Sign (Teahupo'o village, Taiarapu-Ouest)
selfie_spots.detail: at the wave sign on the road in Teahupo'o village, where you can park
selfie_spots.why: A Tripadvisor reviewer called the sign a good photo stop on the road, and the page notes vendors there can take visitors out toward the reef.

ask_someone_spot.name: Teahupo'o village beach, facing the reef
ask_someone_spot.detail: on the beach in Teahupo'o village, standing so the surf break and reef are in view behind you

selfie_research.safety: Never attempt to walk on the reef.
selfie_research.notes: Only one selfie spot was supported by a page that names a findable place. The Wave Sign page does not say the wave is behind the visitor, so the 'best selfie' claim is a reviewer's remark, not a confirmed framing. The beach viewpoint is described only as 'the beach looking out towards the reef'; no specific beach name was found, so the passer-by spot is approximate. Pages found no rules on selfie sticks or tripods. A second selfie spot could not be verified from the pages found.

card.hook: Picture turning on the spot and seeing the whole of Tahiti, then the Pacific, then Mo'orea on the horizon. That's the summit of Mount Orohena, and you earn it with a two- to three-day trek.
card.stand_here: Stand on the summit outcrop of Mount Orohena, about 340 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. On a clear day you get a 360-degree view over the valleys, the coast, Mo'orea and the Pacific.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x for the full sweep of valleys and sea, then 1x for everyday shots. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out Mo'orea and the coastline.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the far land, then drag the slider down a little to make it darker, so the bright cloud and sea keep their detail.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the clouds are usually lower. One guide suggests May to September for clearer skies.
card.selfie_here: Try the Papenoo Valley (Maroto Valley), where a visitor photo shows Mount Orohena clearly in the distance. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the peak over your shoulder. The exact stop isn't named, so look for an open view up the valley, like a spot along the valley road or a riverside clearing.
card.ask_someone: At Point Vénus on the north coast, ask a passer-by to frame you with Mount Orohena behind you, and check the framing together when you arrive.
card.rules_and_safety: Be mindful of your footing when you stop for photos, especially on the trail. The summit trek is best done with a guide, so check with a local guide operator before you go.
card.challenge: Turn slowly on the spot and take one wide shot in each direction, then see if you can spot Mo'orea on the horizon.
card.good_to_know: Mount Orohena is the highest point on Tahiti and in all of French Polynesia, at 2,241 metres (7,352 ft). It's an extinct shield volcano. It ranks 7th in the world for topographic isolation, which means it stands well apart from other high ground, so the view reaches far.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the summit outcrop of Mount Orohena, about 340 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. On a clear day you get a 360-degree view over the valleys, the coast, Mo'orea and the Pacific.

selfie_spots.name: Vallée de Papenoo (Maroto Valley), Tahiti
selfie_spots.detail: Inside the Papenoo valley, in a spot with an open view up the valley; the page does not name a exact stop, so a spot along the valley road or a riverside clearing is the likely setup
selfie_spots.why: A visitor photo from this valley shows Mount Orohena clearly in the distance, so a selfie with the peak behind is possible here.

ask_someone_spot.name: Point Vénus
ask_someone_spot.detail: Stand at Point Vénus on the north coast and have the passer-by frame you with Mount Orohena in the background; the page only gives the view's name, so confirm the exact framing on arrival

sources.title: Orohena from Point Venus (Flickr, by Zeta_Ori)

selfie_research.safety: Be mindful of your footing when stopping for photos, especially on the trail.
selfie_research.notes: Only two sources name a photo location, and neither describes a dedicated selfie stop. The Papenoo entry is a photo of the valley rather than a named selfie spot, and the Point Vénus entry is a Flickr photo title with no details. Pito Iti and the summit outcrop were rejected: from Pito Iti the summit is in front of the visitor rather than behind, and the summit and north-face ledge are trekking points with no map-findable name. No page states rules about selfie sticks or tripods. The 'Be mindful of your footing' safety point comes from a hiking guide, so it is only an on-trail caution.

card.hook: Here's a plot twist: the star of the view outside Papeete Market isn't the market, it's Moorea floating across the water behind it. Treat the building as the setting and you'll get a much better shot.
card.stand_here: Walk north-east to the Boulevard Pomare waterfront, on the stretch directly in front of the market doors. Face the harbour so you get the market's harbour-side facade, the boulevard in the foreground and Moorea on the horizon.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the facade, the boulevard and Moorea all in one frame. Then try 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look at the building, and 2x or more (depending on your phone) to pull Moorea closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on the top or bottom line and keep your phone level so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when a guide says Moorea looks sharp across the water. The market is busiest early, so expect crowds in the aisles. The boulevard is calmer once you've finished shopping.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Boulevard Pomare waterfront right outside the market doors and stand near the entrances with the market behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone has it, to fit more of the building in.
card.rules_and_safety: Market opening times can change, so check Tahiti Tourisme for the current times before you go.
card.challenge: Take one frame of the facade and Moorea, then one of the colourful stalls, and see if you can make them look like they're from two different trips.
card.good_to_know: Papeete Market is the big municipal market in the middle of Papeete, the capital of Tahiti. Stalls sell fruit, vegetables, fish, oils, hats, handbags, local textiles and shell necklaces. For a second picture, go up inside for a wide, high view over the produce, fish and flower stalls below.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk north-east to the Boulevard Pomare waterfront, on the stretch directly in front of the market doors. Face the harbour so you get the market's harbour-side facade, the boulevard in the foreground and Moorea on the horizon.

selfie_spots.name: Waterfront Promenade (Boulevard Pomare), outside the market doors
selfie_spots.detail: on the harbour boulevard that runs along the front of the market building, standing near its entrances so the market is behind you
selfie_spots.why: A travel guide says the harbour boulevard runs straight in front of the market doors and recommends lingering there after shopping.

sources.title: Marché de Papeete - Visit (Papeete, France), 2026 Travel Tips

selfie_research.notes: Only one page names a place next to the market, and it describes the boulevard as being in front of the doors without saying which way to face, so 'market behind you' is my inference. Its main photo suggestion is the Moorea view from that boulevard, not a shot framing the market. No page I found names a specific spot where a passer-by can capture the whole building, so ask_someone_spot is null. The Access Travel and Tahiti Tourisme pages describe the exterior and stalls but give no named viewpoint. No page mentions selfie stick or tripod rules, and none gives a safety point for this market. The given coordinates were not checked against any page.

card.hook: Picture a Japanese-style building sitting among the greenery of Papeari, right across from the Botanical Gardens. It's a museum for Paul Gauguin, and the building is a great photo subject before you even go in.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the Paul Gauguin Museum, where the phone icon sits on the map (PK 51, Papeari, directly across from the Botanical Gardens). Face the building and step back until the whole frontage fits with some greenery around it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the building and its garden. Use zoom 0.5x only if you have to stand close, and keep the building in the middle so the edges don't stretch. Then try zoom 2x or higher, depending on your phone, for a façade detail or the roofline.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the roof and walls up with them so the building looks straight, then tap the building and slide brighter or darker if the sky washes out the walls.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives softer light and gentler shadows on the walls. An overcast day works too, because the greens look rich and even.
card.selfie_here: Try the garden beside the museum, next to the stone tiki figures, with your front camera. There's no promise the building will sit behind you from there, so check the frame before you click. You can also take one on the beach by the water, facing Tahiti-iti.
card.ask_someone: If the grounds are open, ask someone to take your photo in the outdoor courtyard in front of the museum building, and have them step back so the roofline fits in.
card.rules_and_safety: The museum has been closed for renovation, and some visitors have reported it closed, with the adjoining botanical garden closed too. Check the official site before you go, and respect any signs or barriers while you take photos.
card.challenge: Tell the story in three photos: one wide shot of the building and garden, one close-up of a doorway or plant, and one of the entrance sign.
card.good_to_know: The museum is devoted to the life and work of Paul Gauguin in Tahiti. Its exhibits cover French Polynesian and Marquesan culture, with original documents, photographs, reproductions, sculptures, engravings and gouaches. It closed in 2013 for renovation, and a sister museum in Hiva Oa is open.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the Paul Gauguin Museum, where the phone icon sits on the map (PK 51, Papeari, directly across from the Botanical Gardens). Face the building and step back until the whole frontage fits with some greenery around it.

selfie_spots.detail: in the garden next to the museum building, beside the stone tiki figures
selfie_spots.why: A visitor photo of the garden tiki beside the museum is the most specific photo spot a page names, though no page says it is the best angle with the building behind.

ask_someone_spot.name: Exterior courtyard of the Paul Gauguin Museum
ask_someone_spot.detail: in the outdoor courtyard in front of the museum building

selfie_research.notes: The museum is at PK 51 in Papeari on the south-east coast, not in Papeete, so it is an hour or more from the city centre by car. Several reviews from 2015 to 2018 say the museum is closed and abandoned, and one says the adjoining botanical garden was also closed, so check whether it is open before going. No page I found names a spot where the museum is directly behind the visitor, so the selfie spots are based on named photo locations and may not frame the building. No page I found gives rules on selfie sticks or tripods. The ask-someone spot is a courtyard named only in a photo caption, not a stated best viewpoint.

card.hook: Black sand sounds like a joke until you see it: dark beach, green palms, turquoise water, and a white-and-red lighthouse standing in the middle like it's waiting for its photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on the beach in front of the lighthouse at Point Venus and face east towards the tower. You'll get the lighthouse among the palms and black volcanic sand, with turquoise water behind or beside it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the classic shot with a palm on each side. Try 0.5x if you want more sand and sea (keep the horizon level), or 2x-5x for a tighter shot of the tower, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the lighthouse on one of the vertical lines, then tap the lighthouse and slide a little darker so the white tower keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go early, before the cruise-ship day visitors arrive. One guide suggests 6-7am, when the beach is quieter and the light is softer. Golden hour is another popular time.
card.selfie_here: Walk onto the black-sand beach a few yards past the lighthouse, on the way down from the parking lot to the shore. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the lighthouse over your shoulder, with the ocean and Moorea's silhouette in front of you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the shoreline or beach by the lighthouse while you stand on the black sand with the tower behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The sun is strong here, so bring a wide-brimmed hat and sunscreen. The grounds are free to enter, but rules can change, so check locally if you want to do more than walk and take photos.
card.challenge: Crouch low, tuck a palm into the foreground and put the lighthouse on a gridline, so the tower looks a few floors taller than it is.
card.good_to_know: Captain James Cook anchored in Matavai Bay on 12 April 1769 to observe the Transit of Venus. His party set up an observatory and a fortified camp here, and that's how Point Venus got its name. The lighthouse isn't staffed any more, but it's well looked after.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the beach in front of the lighthouse at Point Venus and face east towards the tower. You'll get the lighthouse among the palms and black volcanic sand, with turquoise water behind or beside it.

selfie_spots.name: Black-sand beach just past the lighthouse, toward the water
selfie_spots.detail: On the sand a few yards beyond the lighthouse, on the way from the parking lot down to the shore, with the lighthouse behind you
selfie_spots.why: From here the lighthouse stays behind you while the ocean and Moorea's silhouette fill the view in front.

ask_someone_spot.name: Black-sand beach beside the Point Venus lighthouse
ask_someone_spot.detail: Photograph from the shoreline or beach by the lighthouse, since the tower stands just feet from the black-sand beach. The pages don't give an exact standing point for the passer-by.

sources.title: 10 Amazing Spots for a Photoshoot in Tahiti
54 Best Sights in Tahiti, French Polynesia (Fodor's)

selfie_research.safety: Bring a wide-brimmed hat and sunscreen to stay protected from strong sun.
selfie_research.notes: Only one selfie spot was clearly named by a page; the second-best candidate, the area around the lighthouse, was too vague to give a specific place. The ask-someone spot is an inference from 'photograph by the lighthouse or along the shore' and 'stands just feet away from the beach', so the exact standing point is not confirmed. No page I found gave selfie stick or tripod rules. Sources describe the lighthouse differently (red-and-white in one, whitewashed in another) and give different build years (1867 vs 1868), but these don't change the spots.

card.hook: Picture a wide stone necklace, a pair of carved figures and a lot of green leaves keeping watch. That's Moana, and she's the star of the quieter, better photo at 'Ārahurahu Marae.
card.stand_here: Follow the path to the Moana statue. The phone icon on the map is right beside her. Face her so her wide necklace fills your screen and Heiata stands a little way behind her.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the Moana close-up. Try 2x or more if you want Heiata tucked in closer behind her. Switch to 0.5x when you're at the edge of the pathway and want the long stone path in one go.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, tap Moana's face, then slide it a touch darker if the bright sky behind her is making the carving look washed out.
card.best_time: Earlier or later in the day gives softer light on the carving and stonework. In bright midday sun the tree cover can throw harsh patches, so check each shot on your screen.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the grass beside the two stone guardian statues where you walk in. Use the front camera and try 0.5x so a statue fits over your shoulder with you. No page calls this the best selfie spot, but it's the most clearly photo-worthy one.
card.rules_and_safety: The stone platforms are sacred, so don't walk or climb on them. Shoot from the paths and the edges of the grounds, keep children off the stones, and don't touch the statues. Keep your voice low and your pace slow.
card.challenge: Can you get Moana's necklace sharp and Heiata softly blurred behind her, with not a single stranger in the shot?
card.good_to_know: 'Ārahurahu Marae is a restored sacred site in the Paea area on Tahiti's west coast, in the Tefa'aiti valley. The grounds have stone platforms, a pathway and a courtyard, and the two statues, Moana and Heiata, are replicas. Entry is reported as free with parking nearby, but check the official site before you go in case that has changed.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Follow the path to the Moana statue. The phone icon on the map is right beside her. Face her so her wide necklace fills your screen and Heiata stands a little way behind her.

selfie_spots.name: Guardian tiki statues at the marae entrance
selfie_spots.detail: beside the two stone guardian statues where visitors enter, standing on the grass and not on the stones
selfie_spots.why: The entrance statues greet visitors and are described as photo-worthy, so posing beside them is the most clearly sourced option, though no page names it as the best selfie backdrop.

selfie_research.safety: One reviewer asks visitors to keep children off the stones and rock structures and not to climb on them.
selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a selfie spot with the marae behind the visitor, and none names a spot where a passer-by should photograph a visitor with the whole landmark, so ask_someone_spot is null. The entrance-statue spot is my inference from the statues' location, not a page's recommendation. Pages say visitors may not walk on the sacred stone space and that the statues must not be touched, so keep posing off the stones. No page mentions selfie sticks or tripods. The stone ahu at the rear is the main backdrop named, but it is off-limits to climbing and standing on the sacred space. Marae Arahurahu is in Paea on Tahiti's west coast, not the city centre, so the coordinates given are close to the site.
